extracted.intended_audience: taxpayers, tax professionals, employers, platforms, and digital content creators affected by section 224 (qualified tips) regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Final Treasury/IRS regulations and commentary implementing section 224's deduction for qualified tips, explaining definitions, eligibility, reporting, anti‑abuse rules, exclusions, and examples for taxpayers and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital content creator payments: access versus voluntary payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Customer payments that enable customers to gain access to a creator's content are not tips but compensation; voluntary customer payments made after the customer already gained access are tips because the payment was not required to access content and was voluntary and determined by the customer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations include two examples clarifying when payments to digital content creators are tips vs compensation. Payments that are required to obtain content access are compensation; voluntary payments after access are qualified tips if other requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superficial digital rewards do not disqualify tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Tipping digital content creators through audience engagement mechanisms that result in superficial digital rewards (e.g., highlighted messages or other digital tokens of appreciation that are negligible in value) does not disqualify an otherwise qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations provide an example involving digital content creators and audience engagement. The key is that the digital reward is negligible in value and the payment is voluntary and in excess of any expected payment for services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform retention of tip amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a host platform retains a portion of a user's payment, the retained portion is not received by the individual content creator and is not a qualified tip; platform hosting is not equivalent to content creation and platforms are not on the List of Occupations that Receive Tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 224(d)(1) defines qualified tips as cash tips received by an individual. The term 'individual' does not include an entity that facilitates payment or transmits amounts between customers and service providers. No change made in response to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required reporting to qualify (information return/Form 4137)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts received as a tip are eligible for the section 224 deduction only if they are included on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(3), 6041A(e)(3), 6050W(f)(2), or 6051(a)(18), or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (or successor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amounts not separately reported to an individual on such statements or reported on Form 4137 are not eligible for the deduction under section 224. Issues of creating new reporting mechanisms for independent contractors are beyond the scope of these regulations. See Notice 2025-69 for transition rules related to 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner receipt of tips reported to partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: If a tip received by a partner is reported on an information return provided to the partnership (not to the individual partner), the partner cannot claim the amount as a deduction under section 224 because only qualified tips included in a statement furnished to an 'individual' are allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations follow the statute: statements must be furnished to the individual. No change was made in response to this comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation eligibility (List of Occupations that Receive Tips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tip amounts are only eligible for the deduction if received in an occupation that is on the List of Occupations that Receive Tips (i.e., occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an individual works in two occupations (one on the list and one not), the individual may claim the qualified tip amounts received in the occupation on the list (assuming other requirements are met) but not amounts received in the occupation not on the list. If both occupations are on the list, tip amounts from both occupations may be claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of cash tips (included forms of payment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cash tips are tips received from customers, or through mandatory or voluntary tip-sharing arrangements, that are paid in a cash medium of exchange, including cash, check, credit card, debit card, gift card, tangible or intangible tokens readily exchangeable for a fixed amount in cash (e.g., casino chips), and other forms of electronic settlement or mobile payment denominated in cash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed definition excluded items paid in any medium other than cash (e.g., event tickets, meals, services, or other assets not exchangeable for a fixed cash amount, such as most digital assets). Final regs largely retain the proposed definition and clarify foreign currency is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign currency treated as cash tips
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of section 224, cash tips include amounts paid in foreign currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations explicitly clarify inclusion of foreign-sourced tip amounts and domestic-sourced tip amounts paid in foreign currency as cash tips (subject to other requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital assets excluded from cash tips (including stablecoins pending rulemaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: All digital assets (as defined in section 6045(g)(3)(D) and §1.6045-1(a)(19)) are excluded from the definition of cash tips in these final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasury/IRS will consider tax treatment of payment stablecoins in connection with implementation of the GENIUS Act and may revise rules if payment stablecoins are treated as cash/cash equivalents for other federal tax purposes or legislation changes characterization. If need arises, additional guidance will be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-commerce voluntary surcharges depend on occupation of tip recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a voluntary surcharge added to an e-commerce purchase is a qualified tip depends on the occupation of the tip recipient and whether all other requirements for qualified tips are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a customer commissions an artist on an e-commerce site and includes a cash tip when providing payment, the cash tip is a qualified tip if the occupation (artist) is on the List of Occupations that Receive Tips and other requirements are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary charitable donations are not qualified tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary charitable donations, including donations to community websites for the benefit of an individual or group, are not qualified tips because they are not amounts paid to an individual in excess of an expected or agreed-upon amount for a service provided in an arm's-length transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such amounts are treated as donations, not tips, for section 224 purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified service trade or business (SSTB) exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts received by an individual in the course of a specified service trade or business (as defined in section 199A(d)(2) and §1.199A-5(b)) are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regs would apply this rule without regard to whether an owner can claim a section 199A deduction. Treasury/IRS requested comments on applying §1.199A-5(b) rules to section 224. Final regs reserve subsection (g) for guidance on this exclusion and provided transition relief in Notice 2025-69 until final regs on SSTB determination are issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition relief for SSTB determination (Notice 2025-69)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice 2025-69 provided transition relief: until January 1 of the first calendar year following issuance of final regulations regarding SSTB determination for section 224, IRS will treat taxpayers in occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024 as having received tips in a trade or business that is not an SSTB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transition period is for IRS enforcement and administration to give taxpayers time to determine eligibility. Treasury/IRS intend to issue proposed regulations and solicit comments before publishing final regulations on SSTB issues for section 224.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for amounts received for illegal activities, prostitution, and pornographic activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts received for services the performance of which is a felony or misdemeanor under applicable law, amounts received for prostitution services, and amounts received for pornographic activity are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion is grounded in section 224(d)(2)(C) and (g) authority to prevent noncompliance and abuse. Treasury/IRS may consider additional guidance on these exclusions. If federal law changes (e.g., making certain marijuana transactions lawful), tip amounts in those transactions may become qualified if other requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-abuse general rule (recharacterization of income)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amount is not a qualified tip if, based on all relevant facts and circumstances, the amount represents a recharacterization of wages or payments for goods or services for purposes of claiming the deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasury/IRS replaced a more categorical prohibition with this facts-and-circumstances standard to prevent reclassification of non-tip income as tips. The regs list indicia that may signal recharacterization (see related entries). Audit selection/enforcement procedures are beyond the scope of the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts indicating recharacterization (indicative circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and circumstances that may indicate a recharacterization of wages/payments as tips include: (1) a charge for services on an invoice is less than the payment shown on a related receipt or information return and the cash tip reported approximates the difference; and (2) a significant shift in historical tipping or payment practices between the payor and the tip recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are illustrative indicia; presence of such facts may support a determination that an amount is not a qualified tip under the anti‑abuse rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrebuttable presumption of recharacterization (employer/payor ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an irrebuttable presumption that an amount reflects a recharacterization of wages/payment as tips (and thus cannot be a qualified tip) if: (1) the employer of an employee is the payor of a cash tip received by the employee; or (2) the tip recipient has a direct ownership interest in the payor of a cash tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regs define ownership interest thresholds (corporation: 5%+ vote or value; partnership: 5% profits or capital interest; other: >5% beneficial interest). Ownership is tested on date tip is received. Certain indirect ownership through disregarded entities, QSub, grantor trusts, custodians/agents are treated as direct ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of payor and conduit rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'payor' is defined as the ultimate recipient of the services (usually the customer, client, or other service recipient). An entity that acts merely as a conduit to remit a tip (e.g., employer, third-party settlement organization, sole proprietorship or single-member LLC acting only to remit) is not the payor for these purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements furnished to a sole proprietorship or single‑member LLC that does not elect corporate treatment are considered furnished to the tip recipient owner of that entity, regardless of whether the entity's name appears on the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tip-sharing arrangements included but subject to occupation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224(d)(3) and the final regulations include tips received under any tip-sharing arrangement (mandatory or voluntary) within 'cash tips.' However, participation in a tip-sharing arrangement by itself is not sufficient; the employee must receive tips in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024 and satisfy all other statutory/regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations retain language including tips received through tip-sharing. No additional guidance was added on employees not specifically listed in the List of Occupations that Receive Tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws on tip pooling do not affect federal deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224 is a federal income tax deduction and does not impact Federal or State laws concerning tip-sharing arrangements such as tip pooling; individuals are not precluded from claiming the deduction because of state restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tip-sharing rules are a function of existing laws outside the scope of these regulations, no language was added to preempt or change state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual deduction cap and income phase-out
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224(b)(1) limits the deduction for qualified tips to an amount not to exceed $25,000 in a taxable year. Section 224(b)(2) provides a phase‑out based on modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) over $150,000 ($300,000 for joint filers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations maintain the $25,000 maximum per return (not per spouse) and the statutory MAGI phase-out. Comment requests for indexing or higher caps were not adopted because statute does not provide for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Married filing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224(f) provides that if the taxpayer is a married individual, section 224 applies only if the taxpayer and spouse file a joint return for the taxable year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations retain the rule requiring married individuals to file jointly to be eligible for the deduction, consistent with statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid SSN requirement to claim deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim a deduction under section 224, a taxpayer must include on the return a valid for work Social Security Number (SSN) that was issued before the due date of the return (including extensions). Married taxpayers must include the valid SSN of the spouse who received the tips; both SSNs are required only when both spouses have qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is statutory. Income tax return instructions will include examples for married taxpayers and scenarios (e.g., moving from ITIN to SSN). Comments suggesting ITIN safe harbors or other exceptions were not adopted.
